title: Esther Before the King, Haman at Home
summary: On the third day Esther enters the inner court in her royal robes, and the king holds out the gold scepter and offers her up to half the kingdom. Instead of making her request, she invites the king and Haman to a banquet, and there she invites them to a second banquet the next day. Haman leaves elated but is enraged by Mordecai's refusal to honor him, and on the advice of his wife Zeresh and his friends he builds a gallows fifty cubits high for Mordecai.
story: Esther ended chapter 4 by resolving to go to the king though it might cost her life. Here the danger passes in two verses: she finds favor, and the scepter is extended. But the rescue is not accomplished yet, and the chapter slows the story down deliberately. Esther does not blurt out her request; she sets a table, and then another. Meanwhile the narrative cuts to Haman's house, where his pride and his hatred of Mordecai push him toward a fatal overreach. By the end of the chapter two lines are converging on the next morning: Esther's second banquet, where she will speak, and Haman's plan to ask the king for Mordecai's death.
historical:
The scene is again the palace at Susa in the reign of Xerxes (486 to 465 BC). The king sits on his throne in the royal hall facing the entrance, which matches what is known of Persian audience halls, large columned rooms in which the king was seen from a distance and approached with ceremony. The offer of up to half the kingdom was a formula of royal generosity rather than a literal promise; Herod Antipas makes the same kind of offer in the Gospels (Mark 6:23), and no one would have expected a Persian king to divide his empire at a banquet.

The gallows is fifty cubits high. A cubit was the length of a forearm, roughly eighteen inches, so the structure would be about seventy-five feet tall, a deliberately exaggerated height meant to be seen across the city. The Hebrew word is simply tree or wood, and many scholars think it refers to a stake for impaling or displaying a body rather than a rope gallows. Persian kings are known to have used impalement for rebels and traitors; Darius I records it in his Behistun inscription, and Herodotus reports it as well.
cultural:
Banquets carry much of Esther's plot. The book opens with Xerxes' feasts (chapter 1), and in this chapter Esther uses the banquet as a tool of diplomacy. To invite the king to a meal she had prepared was to honor him and to draw him into a setting where a request could be made gracefully. Wine was central to Persian feasting, and the king makes his offer to Esther again as they drink. Esther's double invitation keeps the king curious and signals that her request is serious. It also lets her include Haman, placing the enemy at the queen's table where he can be exposed.

Haman's speech to his family shows how honor worked in an ancient court. Wealth, many sons, and promotion over other officials were the visible measures of a man's standing, and a public slight from an inferior could feel intolerable. Mordecai's refusal to rise or tremble before him at the king's gate, the place where officials sat and business was done, is a public act that Haman takes as an insult to all his glory.
literary: The chapter has two halves, the queen's court (verses 1-8) and Haman's house (verses 9-14), and they are set against each other. In the first, Esther is composed and patient; she speaks with the formal courtesy of the court, repeating the phrases found favor and if it pleases the king. In the second, Haman lists his glory at length and then confesses that none of it satisfies him while he sees Mordecai. The storyteller uses delay as suspense: the king asks for her request three times across chapters 5 and 7, and the reader must wait. There is irony throughout. Haman boasts that he alone is invited with the king, not knowing that the invitation is a trap, and he ends the day pleased with a gallows that will be used for him.

outline.t: Esther enters the court and finds favor
The first banquet and the invitation to a second
Haman's joy turns to rage at Mordecai
Haman boasts of his glory to his family
Zeresh advises a gallows for Mordecai

doctrines.note: Esther finds favor at the moment her life is at stake, and the delay she chooses sets up the events of the coming night. The book shows ordinary human decisions, wise and foolish, being gathered into a larger plan that none of the characters can see.

Haman is a study in pride and resentment. He has wealth, family, and honor, yet one man's refusal to bow poisons all of it. His discontent shows how pride always needs more and how hatred can make a person reckless.
Esther acts with patience and discretion rather than haste. Her timing reflects the wisdom tradition's regard for speaking the right word at the right moment.

words.note: Chen, favor or grace, the goodwill one person finds in another's sight. Esther found favor with all who saw her and with the king earlier in the book (2:15, 17), and here she finds favor again at the moment she most needs it. The same word describes the grace Noah found in the eyes of the LORD (Genesis 6:8).

Mishteh, feast or banquet, literally a drinking. The word appears more often in Esther than in any other book, and the plot moves from feast to feast: the king's feasts, Esther's two banquets, and finally the feasting of Purim.

Shavah, to be like, to be worth or equal to. Haman says that all his wealth and honor is worth nothing to him (verse 13) while Mordecai sits at the gate. His words expose how one grudge can empty a life of its satisfactions.

Ets, tree or wood, here a stake or gallows. The same word is used for trees throughout the Old Testament. The structure Haman builds is likely a tall pole for execution or public display, and the word will recur until it is used for Haman himself.

christ: The chapter's movement from danger to favor, and from a hidden plan to a coming reversal, belongs to a pattern that runs through the Bible and reaches its fullest form in the gospel. Some readers note that Esther goes in on the third day, but that phrase marks time here and should not be pressed into a prophecy of the resurrection. What the chapter does show clearly is the self-destroying nature of pride: Haman builds the instrument of his own death while plotting another's. Jesus taught that those who exalt themselves will be humbled, and Mary's song celebrates the God who “has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble” (Luke 1:52). Christ is the one who did not grasp at glory but humbled himself, and whom God exalted.
questions: Esther waits instead of making her request at once. When have you seen patience or good timing accomplish what haste could not?
Haman says that none of his blessings satisfies him while Mordecai sits at the gate. What grudge or comparison is most likely to steal your contentment?
Zeresh and Haman's friends feed his anger instead of checking it. What kind of friends help you see your own pride honestly?
